title: Monopoly Round-Up: The AI Bubble Pop is Going to Claim More Victims
author: Matt Stoller
content:
This is the weekly Monopoly Round-Up, where we aggregate all of the Good and
Bad monopoly-related news of the week. As usual, there was a lot, involving
major lawsuits against prediction markets, aka "gambling," and against OpenAI
in connection with hacking Hugging Face in July. The number of loss-of-control
incidents based on OpenAI models is far more than has been publicly disclosed.

All of that is below, for paid subscribers only. But before we get to that,
Matt is back to discuss the ongoing AI crash, prompted by Nvidia CEO Jensen
Huang's resignation and the failed initial public offering of Anthropic.

On Friday, the NASDAQ fell by more than five percent, sliding into what is
known as a 'correction.' The rest of the market dropped as well, as have
commodities. Just what is going on? Why now? How bad is it likely to be? And
will this financial morass affect the 'real' economy? That's what this column
will try to answer.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!2Ilw!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ffcd00a45-c657-48b3-8b3f-3ef2b45616c7_688x501.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!2Ilw!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ffcd00a45-c657-48b3-8b3f-3ef2b45616c7_688x501.png)

The signs of an AI bubble have been ominous for years. Steve Eisman, who
predicted the 2008 crisis,
[says](https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/articles/one-trade-steve-
eisman-warns-114500717.html) a good chunk of medium-sized AI companies, the
'neoclouds,' are going to zero, and added that nearly the entire stock market
is linked to the AI trade. Many of the other icons of that earlier crisis,
like Michael Burry, have said something similar. But there is a deep consensus
underpinning the constant rise in value of financial assets, and that
consensus had not come under strain until a few months ago.

Then, over the past few months, something snapped. About a month ago, BIG
noted that the [bubble had started to
deflate](https://www.thebignewsletter.com/p/monopoly-round-up-pop-the-damn-
ai), pointing to the collapse of financing for leading AI chip firm Nvidia's
off-balance sheet entities, known as neoclouds. Since that date, those
neocloud stock prices have fallen by more than half, with their debt at junk
levels. And Nvidia's market value is down by three trillion dollars.

On Friday, we finally had real panic. For instance, two minutes after the
close of the stock market, software giant Oracle tweeted out a message
explaining, unprompted, that they were fully solvent and had all the financing
they need. "Any media reports that will come out and say the contrary," it
said, "are incorrect and wrong."

It was a disconcerting message for two reason. First Oracle, a reliable
company since its founding in the 1970s, had fallen to a 52-week low and its
credit default swaps, basically the bet traders make on whether the company
will default on its debt, went parabolic. Second and more importantly, no one
asked. Typically, you don't adamantly deny a charge no one has made unless
something is wrong. ("Hey honey just so you know I set up a dating profile for
no reason and I absolutely am not looking around to hook up with others…")

A major company like Oracle announcing such a creepy denial is panic.

So what can we expect? Well, there's hope this isn't a bear market, but a
temporary pullback before the markets go higher. And I suppose that's possible
if the Federal Reserve takes radical action, but I suspect it won't. We're
likely in a bear market. And bear markets don't typically end with a violent
downturn, they end after a long period of volatility. We may see a bounce on
Monday, but a key part of a crash dynamic is the bear market bounce, fierce
rallies upward that convince speculators the market has hit a bottom. After
such a rally, the market resumes its slide. Six of the top ten biggest daily
gains on the Nasdaq [took
place](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_largest_daily_changes_in_the_Nasdaq_Composite)
during the dot com bust or 2008 crisis. When enough speculators get bored and
lose hope after buying into a bear market rally, the bear market ends.

Crashes take time to play out. During the dot com bust, for instance, the
Nasdaq started declining in March of 2000 and took until October of 2002 to
hit its low, declining a full 78%. The Dow declined much less and started
falling later, and the country didn't hit a recession until a year after the
tech stocks declined, when the IT spending cuts slammed into the rest of the
economy. Something similar happened in the great financial crisis; the
subprime mortgage lenders started dropping in 2006, the full crash didn't
manifest until 2008.

In this case, it seems like the AI trade is over, and with it, big parts of
our financial system may blow up.

So what exactly is starting to pop this bubble? It's likely borrowing costs.
Speculators are businesses, and their cost of inventory is the price of money.
If that goes up, it's harder to bet, and more of them are forced to sell. The
10-year Treasury bond increased by about 30%, from 4% in February of this year
to 5.27% at its height. That's a big hike in the price of money.

Here's a chart of the Treasury yield, which is the benchmark for most
borrowing. It's been rising all year. This increase is a result of the war in
Iran, borrowing by data centers and governments, and the Federal Reserve's
decision to tighten rates due to fears over inflation. Every trader or fund
now has to pay higher amounts to trade, which creates more fragility in their
balance sheets.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Qc30!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F71bb3f8c-c207-49e5-9435-633ad1f6f055_700x494.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Qc30!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F71bb3f8c-c207-49e5-9435-633ad1f6f055_700x494.png)

These borrowing costs have been hammering the market for months; hedge funds
have been blowing up since the summer. For instance, the $45 billion AI-
focused fund Situational Awareness [had to sell
much](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/07/31/why-leopold-aschenbrenner-situational-
awareness-hedge-fund-imploded.html) of its portfolio in July.

### Other People's Money

To understand the deflating of this bubble, let's separate the two different
phenomena comprising it. The first is statistical inference technology known
as AI, and the second is finance. What links them is that the corporations
that house AI technology, and the various expensive aspects of it, such as
chips, land, electricity, and water, are using a financial model that does not
bring in the cash to cover their debt service costs. For a time, that didn't
matter, they simply borrowed more money to make up the difference, in the
hopes that the revenue would show up eventually. That hasn't happened, and now
there's a credit crunch.

All bubbles have one important characteristic; they involve gambling with
other people's money. And that borrowed money will show up somewhere. Last
week, I finally figured out where the borrowing is happening: hedge funds. The
Federal Reserve published its semi-annual [financial stability
report](https://www.federalreserve.gov/publications/files/financial-stability-
report-20261113.pdf), and it included a series of charts showing that the
hedge fund sector is more leveraged than it has been since 2013. The gross
asset value of the hedge fund sector is $13 trillion, whereas the net asset
value is just $4 trillion. That's a lot of leverage! And it's concentrated in
the larger trading firms like Jane Street and Citadel.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!imtU!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-

post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe5efb0b5-d125-4eff-a251-28d022ce06a4_527x542.png)

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!1_Du!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-

post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0494f0fb-3c81-4529-81d8-98bf0cd6c598_584x250.png)

The Financial Times
[discussed](https://www.ft.com/content/d313d0ce-d552-463e-9e84-6fa8c3efeeec?syn-25a6b1a6=1)
increased borrowing by these institutions in October. The top 15 hedge funds,
according to the FT, borrow eleven dollars for every dollar they manage. And
they borrow it from the big banks, aka Goldman, Morgan Stanley, and JP Morgan,
who are not able to track the concentrated risks of their counterparties.
There are other areas of elevated leverage, such as life insurers.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!yjYa!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F4f344b61-107f-4084-a9f2-80f34b498793_740x472.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!yjYa!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F4f344b61-107f-4084-a9f2-80f34b498793_740x472.png)

You can see that the increase in leverage started in late 2022 and early 2023,
which is both when ChatGPT launched, and when regulators bailed out Silicon
Valley Bank. The SVB bailout had two consequences. First, bailouts tend to
communicate to investors to be more aggressive, and more cautious speculators
lose out. So that bailout told speculators to lever up, because if they
didn't, they would be outcompeted by those who did. And if they did get
reckless, they'd get protection on the downside. Second, a lot of the money in
SVB was crypto money, and that money funded the early AI companies. ChatGPT
was a great excuse to borrow and gamble on this new narrative.

So today, we're sitting with at least $9 trillion of excess leverage that
didn't exist when ChatGPT was first announced. That isn't the same size as the
financial crisis of 2008, where the mortgage mess was $14 trillion. But it's
still a lot of money. And that's just what we know. There's a lot more we
don't know about balance sheets. It's also not important to lay out all of the
places where things _could_ blow up, it's enough to point out that there's a
giant pot of leverage financing higher asset prices. After all, if a bunch of
institutions own a stock with borrowed money, and the bank calls in their
loans, that creates a fire sale of that stock, and then more margin calls.

There's also good news, households haven't been borrowing excessively. That
was most definitely not the case in 2008. Back then, Americans were scared of
what was happening, since so many had mortgages on high-priced housing. Today,
the distance of ordinary people from the actual debt dynamics of the AI bubble
might be one reason it is attracting a sort of broad scorn. California Senator
Adam Schiff, who is not known for being heroic or a threat to big tech, just
[penned](https://www.wsj.com/opinion/no-ai-company-is-too-big-to-
fail-462bf066) an oped in the Wall Street Journal explaining there will be no
bailout this time.

In sum, superrich hedge fund and private equity managers have borrowed
trillions from superrich Wall Street bankers to gamble on trillions of AI
stocks and debt issued by superrich Silicon Valley monopolists to finance
trillions of investment. They have
[peddled](https://www.thebignewsletter.com/p/why-are-we-pretending-ai-is-
going) a host of falsehoods to justify this gambling, like the neoliberal
fantasy that AI would replace all jobs. But while the technology certainly
could be useful, it's entirely unclear whether or how it will be profitable,
or whether these bets will pay out.

### Jensen Huang and the End of Number Go Up

There has also been a slow-motion scandal at AI chipmaker Nvidia, with CEO
Jensen Huang resigning a few weeks ago. Nvidia designs the chips powering
artificial intelligence. The main allegation is he was having an affair with a
Chinese spy and sending powerful chips to China, contra U.S. policy aims. I do
not believe that story is why he resigned, I think it's more likely the board
fired him because he was committing fraud, claiming the sales of chips that
were not in fact being sold. Nvidia has since shed nearly three trillion
dollars in market value; that loss of market capitalization is consistent with
fraud, not espionage. (The company, notably, had accounting scandals in 2003
and 2022.)

Nvidia is a big deal. The psychological shock of Nvidia's collapse is hard to
overstate. It is one of the most successful stocks of the last thirty years.
If you had put $100 into Nvidia when it first went public in 1993, you'd have
roughly a half a million dollars today. Much, though not all, of that increase
is a result of the AI boom of the last four years, and virtually all of it
took place in the zero interest era after the financial crisis.

Last year, I [wrote up](https://www.thebignewsletter.com/p/nvidias-trillions-
why-we-keep-hearing) why we keep hearing about Nvidia, which at 6% of the S&P,
is of structural significance to the U.S. economy and financial system. Nvidia
is a systemically important firm, both in terms of its products and as a
quasi-financial institution.

But its importance is relatively new. Nvidia started in the 1990s as a mid-
level graphics chip company that specialized in improving video games. The
company based its strategy on designing chips that handled graphics, or
graphics processing units (GPUs), versus the then-dominant and lucrative
central processing units (CPUs) that ran the architecture of the personal
computer, which were made by Intel.

Huang was a salesman and stock promoter, and he instilled an aggressive
culture in the company. One of his skills was to build and sell into new
computing paradigms. Nvidia's products were especially useful for crypto
mining, so Huang promoted that space for a time with overwrought rhetoric. He
also understood that machine learning was a great place for graphics
processors; he was at the founding of OpenAI in 2015, handing them chips.

When ChatGPT launched in 2022, the company exploded in importance. As Nvidia
became more important, Huang moved to become a stock promoter and corporate
diplomat pretty much full-time.

His attempt to purchase chip blueprint firm Arm was blocked by Lina Khan's
Federal Trade Commission in 2021. The company is also alleged to have used
monopolistic tactics, locking up supply chains and threatening customers who
consider using rival chips. The Biden administration was in the early stages
of looking into Nvidia for antitrust violations, Europe already had, and it is
now [being probed](https://www.semafor.com/article/11/12/2026/us-doj-probes-
nvidia) by the Federal government on those grounds.

After Trump got elected in 2024, Huang turned to cultivating the President.
Nvidia became the largest donor to the Trump ballroom. But Huang also became
remarkably sycophantic. "America's unique advantage that no other country can
possibly have," [he
said](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2025-07-23/trump-weighed-nvidia-
breakup-before-realizing-it-d-be-hard) in 2025, "is President Trump." Upon the
launch of the war against Iran, he went out of his way to talk up the
conflict. "I believe that there's a reason we went to war," he
[argued](https://x.com/TheChiefNerd/status/2035176931604230311). "And I
believe at the end of the war, the Middle East will be more stable than
before." Like most super aggressive unethical salesmen, Huang didn't know or
care whether that was true. He got what he wanted, which were political favors
like an exemption from Trump's tariffs, and special treatment vis-a-vis China.

And that brings us to China. It has been U.S. policy since the Biden
administration to bar the export of top tier chips to Chinese firms that could
enable the Chinese military to use them. Like it or not, and many reasonable
people do not, those export controls are the law. Huang vehemently opposed
those rules, calling China hawks an embarrassment, lauding the Chinese
government, and even instructing his subordinates to never [even
think](https://x.com/joannachiu/status/1909646827332456926) about the
potential geopolitical risk of locating all production in the hotspot of
Taiwan. While assertive, those moves are not illegal.

What _is_ illegal is the alleged diversion of top Nvidia chips to Chinese
firms such as Megaspeed, which apparently bought tens of billions of chips and
moved them into China. Alice Huang, the ostensible spy, was an official at
Megaspeed. But of course, whether she was a spy or a honeypot seems kind of
besides the point, because Nvidia had its own strong interest in smuggling
those chips. Those interests were twofold. First, Nvidia made money by selling
more chips. But second, having lots of demand for chips allowed the company to
overcharge existing customers, while threatening to withhold chips from
customers that might look elsewhere.

It's not clear how much of the company's revenue depended on this smuggling,
but it could [be as much](https://www.wsj.com/business/earnings/nvidias-
disappearing-singapore-sales-deepen-mystery-around-
megaspeed-7d483180?st=vbWtkd&reflink=desktopwebshare_permalink) as 20-25%.
Here's the Wall Street Journal:

> As recently as the summer of last year, Singapore was officially one of
> Nvidia's biggest markets, generating 22% of the chip maker's revenue. Then,
> practically overnight, it disappeared from the company's financial
> disclosures.

If true, that smells a lot like securities fraud. And it's not the only
incident. There is of course the 'circular financing,' which is Enron-style
off-balance sheet accounting. Nvidia finances its own customers to buy its own
chips as a way of artificially increasing demand. I went over how it did so
with what are called [neoclouds](https://www.thebignewsletter.com/p/monopoly-
round-up-the-cockroaches) like CoreWeave, Nebius and Firmus, who are now
struggling. Nvidia also bought [$10 billion
shares](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/business/anthropic-ipo-nvidia.html)
of Anthropic, which is a customer, in its highly anticipated initial public
offering. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, of all people, implied that Huang
was cooking the books, it's so bad that the corrupt and flabby Trump
Securities and Exchange Commission is
[looking](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/20/business/nvidia-sec-
accounting.html) into Nvidia for accounting fraud.

Throughout the growth of Nvidia, Huang was a lone wolf CEO. Journalists like
to throw around that he had 60 people reporting to him directly, but of
course, no one can have 60 subordinates in any meaningful sense. It's clear he
just did whatever he wanted with weak systems in place, and the gusher of
unexpected money from an AI boom covered up for any problems that might
accrue.

Huang also had a lot of enemies, across the board, accumulating them through
careless activities. His affairs are evidence of that cavalier attitude. When
you have an undisciplined authoritarian CEO thrust into the global spotlight,
and then a wave of money followed by scrutiny and competition, it's not a
surprise you'd find fraud and illegal activity -- and that enemies would
expose it.

Huang's shocking fall means that Nvidia's use of its balance sheet to prop up
AI chip demand is likely over. Anthropic
[needs](https://www.thebignewsletter.com/p/why-anthropics-filing-crushed-tech)
the capital from Nvidia, as do the neoclouds and a whole set of companies that
stir up AI demand. And that means we're going to learn about the real
economics of artificial intelligence, and whether it can sustain the high
equity values underpinning our stock market.

But Nvidia isn't the only major corporation in trouble.

### The Anthropic Rug Pull

On Thursday, the giant AI company Anthropic, which sells its Claude series of
tools, offered shares to the public. The company's technology is great. But as
a corporation, it is wildly unprofitable, its growth is slowing, and it has
nearly a trillion dollars of committed spending on data centers. And it was a
broken initial public offering, with the stock beginning trading at $115
before falling to near its official IPO price of $83 midday on Friday.

The mechanics of what happened in the IPO are interesting and reflect the
behavior of someone who realizes it's the end of a bubble. Wall Street banks
could have priced the stock to help small investors profit, but instead
overreached to maximize the amount going to insiders, who dumped their shares
on the public. If it looked a lot like what is known in crypto parlance as a
'rug pull,' that's because it was. Sam Bankman-Fried of FTX was an early
investor in Anthropic, and the cross-over between crypto, the effective
altruism cult, and generative AI is porous.

Anthropic was supposed to be the savior of the bubble after Nvidia's disgrace,
but it wasn't. That's what Jim Cramer discussed on CNBC, at any rate, hoping
they could just keep the market up until revenue started coming in to service
the debts. And he was very disappointed at the scamming of retail investors
for the benefit of insiders. At BIG, we
[argued](https://www.thebignewsletter.com/p/why-anthropics-filing-crushed-
tech) this attitude was more than just wishful thinking; Anthropic's public
offering was systemic, involving payoffs to the most important people in
Silicon Valley and on Wall Street.

In September, BIG argued that Anthropic's IPO [may end up
crashing](https://www.thebignewsletter.com/p/monopoly-round-up-just-stop-the-
anthropic) the whole space, as it would reveal the poor economics underlying
the entire AI ecosystem. And it looks like that's what happened.

### What Now?

And now let's get back to some of the other key institutions, notably Oracle,
which put up that awkward tweet on Friday.

Oracle is a big database company founded in the 1970s. Its founder, Larry
Ellison, is close with SpaceX's Elon Musk, and his son used his father's
wealth to buy Paramount and Warner. What makes Oracle characteristic of this
bubble is that it is leveraged, meaning it [has
something](https://roddubitsky.substack.com/p/ai-patient-zero-oracles-
investment) like $465 billion of debt and obligations that it likely can't
service. It has negative cash flow of $16 billion a year.

Oracle's hope is that in a few years, it will start making money from its data
centers, and cover its debt load. And on its recent Investor Day presentation,
it said that by 2029 it will have over $30 billion in free cash flow. But the
problem for Oracle is that it's expecting all of that to come from a handful
of customers. And its main customer is OpenAI, which itself is burning cash
and can't raise what it needs.

In OpenAI's last fundraising round, it sought to raise $30 billion from
private investors, but only got $11 billion. Its last hope is the public
markets, but since Anthropic's IPO busted, there's no way OpenAI can go
public. And OpenAI's main backer, the Japanese giant Softbank, is another
giant investment firm that may get taken down because of its massive
indebtedness and bet on AI. And on and on it goes.

In other words, multiple large prestigious companies have intertwined balance
sheets, and have bet everything, and then some, on corporate America spending
large fractions of their revenue on artificial intelligence tools. And now,
the proverbial bank - and the literal banks, too -- may be calling in the
loan.

### The Stakes

In June, BIG [wrote](https://www.thebignewsletter.com/p/what-would-it-look-
like-if-the-ai) up what will likely happen in a collapse, at least in terms of
how the financial contagion will manifest and turn a crash into a downturn.
Consumer spending could drop as portfolios and pensions take a hit.
Significant institutions are likely going to be hurt. We may wind up in
recession, or worse.

Academic institutions and nonprofits will likely lose significant parts of
their portfolios. Cities like New York and states like California that rely on
capital gains taxes will find themselves in real trouble, and South Korea,
Japan, and Taiwan will be damaged. Foreigners who hold U.S. assets, and at
this point that's a significant fraction of U.S. equity holdings, may lose
out, leading to geopolitical tensions and a potential risk for the dollar.
Unlike the dot com bust or the Great Financial Crisis, the U.S. economy is
much less diversified and runs a trade deficit in such basics as food. So
other areas can't pick up the slack, and if we can't keep importing more than
a trillion dollars more goods than we export, we're in real trouble.

Moreover, adjacent frauds will be discovered, as people rush for liquidity.
Bernie Madoff's Ponzi scheme wasn't related to the 2008 financial crisis, but
as people sold what they had to get cash, that was uncovered. It's likely
something will happen with cyberattacks this time, or fraud in fintechs, since
the space is so poorly regulated.

In this scenario there is going to be immense pressure on the political system
to offer a response, perhaps a bailout, but certainly a new national
development strategy, structured by a giant blue wave of Democratic party
populists.

This situation won't happen all at once, it will play out over time. The
specifics are unpredictable. But my guess is that it has started.

Now, on to the Good and Bad News. Congress wants to make progress on
healthcare, which is good, but only if they take on corporate consolidation
and vertical integration. Meanwhile, the Trump Administration is continuing to
run interference for the largest railroad merger in history, the Instacart-
DoorDash merger, and even Kalshi. That and a whole lot after the jump, for
paid subscribers.
